# Why Deep Learning? {background-color="#1a252f"}

## A Step Change {.center}

- In traditional machine learning, humans design the features the model uses
- In deep learning, **the model learns which features matter directly from data**

> The gap closed in 2012: one model changed the trajectory of an entire field.

::: notes
- In 2012, AlexNet entered the ImageNet competition and cut the top-5 error rate nearly in half
- Not an incremental improvement — a signal that the rules had changed
- Given enough data and compute, networks can learn to see in ways that surpass hand-crafted approaches
- Every image recognition system today traces a line back to this moment
:::

## ImageNet Error Rates {.center}

| Year | Model | Top-5 Error |
|------|-------|-------------|
| 2010 | NEC-UIUC | 28.2% |
| 2011 | XRCE | 25.8% |
| **2012** | **AlexNet** | **15.3%** |
| 2014 | VGGNet | 7.3% |
| 2015 | ResNet | 3.6% |

> The step change happened in 2012, and has not stopped since.

::: notes
- 2010–2011: modest, incremental gains, the kind researchers expected
- 2012: AlexNet nearly halves the error rate in a single year
- 2015: ResNet reaches 3.6%, better than most humans on this task
- Once the approach was validated, progress accelerated rapidly and has continued to do so
:::

# The Neuron {background-color="#1a252f"}

## The Building Block {.center}

```{mermaid}
graph LR
  x1["x1 (input 1)"] -->|"x w1"| S["sum"]
  x2["x2 (input 2)"] -->|"x w2"| S
  x3["x3 (input 3)"] -->|"x w3"| S
  S --> A["activation function"]
  A --> out["output"]
```

- Takes in several inputs
- Multiplies each by a **weight** (its importance)
- Passes the weighted sum through an activation function

::: notes
- A neuron takes several inputs, multiplies each by a weight (its importance), and sums them up
- The weighted sum passes through an activation function — output is a single number
- This is the building block; everything in deep learning is built from variations on this
- The maths matters more than the biological metaphor
:::

## Weights Are the Memory {.center}

| Input | Weight | Interpretation |
|-------|--------|----------------|
| Bright region near disc | 0.9 | Strongly relevant |
| Overall image brightness | 0.1 | Weakly relevant |
| Background noise | 0.01 | Almost irrelevant |

- The weights are **learned** during training, they start random
- A high weight: "this input matters for this decision"
- **The network's knowledge lives entirely in its weights**

::: notes
- Before training, weights are random, the network knows nothing
- After training, weights encode what the network has discovered about inputs and outputs
- "Learning" means weights have settled into values that produce good predictions
- The weights are the model — save the weights, save everything the network knows
:::

# Networks and Layers {background-color="#1a252f"}

## Stacking Neurons

:::: {.nn-layout}
::: {.nn-bullets}
- Each layer is a collection of neurons
- Every neuron connects to every neuron in the next layer
- Each layer passes a transformed signal forward
:::
```{mermaid}
graph LR
  subgraph Input
    i1((i1))
    i2((i2))
    i3((i3))
  end
  subgraph Hidden
    h1((h1))
    h2((h2))
    h3((h3))
    h4((h4))
  end
  subgraph Output
    o1((o1))
    o2((o2))
  end
  i1 --> h1
  i1 --> h2
  i1 --> h3
  i1 --> h4
  i2 --> h1
  i2 --> h2
  i2 --> h3
  i2 --> h4
  i3 --> h1
  i3 --> h2
  i3 --> h3
  i3 --> h4
  h1 --> o1
  h1 --> o2
  h2 --> o1
  h2 --> o2
  h3 --> o1
  h3 --> o2
  h4 --> o1
  h4 --> o2
```
::::

::: notes
- Many neurons together form a layer; stacked layers form a network
- Each layer takes the previous layer's outputs and applies a transformation via weights and activations
- The cascade of transformations builds progressively complex representations of the input
:::

## What Each Layer Represents {.center}

| Layer | Role |
|-------|------|
| **Input** | Raw data — pixel values, numbers |
| **Hidden** | Learned representations — patterns, features |
| **Output** | The prediction — class probabilities |

- Hidden layers are named because we do not directly control what they learn
- They discover useful structure in the data on their own

::: notes
- Input layer receives raw data (for images, pixel values) no transformation applied
- Hidden layers build progressively more abstract representations of the input
- Output layer converts those representations into a prediction (class probabilities)
- Called "hidden" because their representations are not directly interpretable — learned, not designed
:::

# Activation Functions {background-color="#1a252f"}

## Without Activation: Just a Line {.center}

- A neural network with no activation functions behaves like **one big linear equation**
- No matter how many layers you add, the output is still a linear function of the input
- You could replace a 100-layer network (without activations) with a single matrix multiplication

::: notes
- Without activations, stacking layers does nothing useful — each is just a linear transformation
- The composition of linear functions is still a linear function
- An entire deep network without activations could be collapsed to a single matrix multiplication
- Linear functions cannot model the complex, non-linear patterns present in real data like images
:::

## Non-Linearity Unlocks Complexity {.center}

```{mermaid}
graph LR
  sum["Weighted sum"] --> relu["ReLU:<br/>negative to 0,<br/>positive unchanged"] --> out["Output"]
```

- Activation functions introduce **non-linearity** after each weighted sum
- The most common today: **ReLU** — simple, effective, fast
- With non-linearity, stacked layers can model functions of arbitrary complexity

::: notes
- ReLU returns zero for negative inputs, passes positive inputs through unchanged
- Simple but enormously effective, the output is not a linear function of the input
- Non-linearity means stacking more layers genuinely increases what the network can model
:::

# The Forward Pass {background-color="#1a252f"}

## How a Prediction is Made {.center}

```{mermaid}
graph LR
  A["Pixel values"] --> B["Layer 1: simple patterns"] --> C["Layer 2: complex patterns"] --> D["Layer 3: task features"] --> E["0.87 disease / 0.13 healthy"]
```

- Data enters at the input layer and flows **forward** through each layer
- Each layer transforms the representation
- The output layer produces the final prediction

::: notes
- Pixel values enter the input layer and flow forward through each hidden layer
- Each layer applies a transformation, building a progressively richer representation
- The output layer distills the representation into a prediction
- One direction only, no loops (hence "forward" pass)
:::

## A Number for Each Class {.center}

| Class | Raw score (logit) | Probability |
|-------|------------------|-------------|
| No disease | 0.55 | 13% |
| **Disease** | **2.1** | **87%** |

- The class with the **highest raw score** is the prediction
- Scores are converted to probabilities using the **softmax** function
- Everything the network has learned collapses into two numbers at the end

::: notes
- Output layer produces two numbers (logits), one for each class
- Softmax converts logits to probabilities that sum to 1
- Highest probability = the prediction
- Everything—all layers, weights, and learned features—collapses into two numbers at the end
:::

# Loss Functions {background-color="#1a252f"}

## How Wrong Are We? {.center}

| Prediction | True label | Loss |
|-----------|-----------|------|
| 90% disease | Disease | Low — correct and confident |
| 55% disease | Disease | Medium — correct but uncertain |
| 20% disease | Disease | High — wrong and confident |

- After a forward pass, we have a prediction and the correct answer (the **label**)
- The **loss function** turns the gap between them into a single number

::: notes
- The loss function takes the prediction and the correct label, returns a number summarising the error
- Loss near zero: accurate prediction; high loss: wrong or uncertain
- Cross-entropy loss penalises confident wrong predictions particularly heavily
- Pushes the network to be appropriately certain only when it has good reason to be
:::

## A Landscape to Navigate {.center}

```{mermaid}
graph LR
  A["Random weights - high loss"] -->|"adjust weights"| B["Better weights - lower loss"] -->|"adjust weights"| C["Good weights - low loss"]
```

- Every set of weights produces a different loss value
- Training is the process of **navigating towards the minimum**
- Think of it as finding the bottom of a valley in a very high-dimensional space

::: notes
- Every combination of weights is a point in a vast space, there is one dimension per weight
- The loss function gives a number at each point: how wrong is the network here?
- Training = moving through this space towards a region of low loss
- The landscape has many local minima but gradient descent finds good solutions reliably in practice
:::

# Learning {background-color="#1a252f"}

## Gradient Descent {.center}

```{mermaid}
graph LR
  A["Random weights"] --> B["Forward pass:<br/>make a prediction"]
  B --> C["Calculate loss:<br/>how wrong?"]
  C --> D["Backward pass:<br/>how much did each<br/>weight contribute?"]
  D --> E["Nudge each weight<br/>to reduce loss"]
  E --> B
```

- Each step nudges every weight a small amount in the direction that reduces loss
- The size of each step is controlled by the **learning rate**

::: notes
- The gradient tells us whether increasing or decreasing each weight would increase or decrease the loss
- Move each weight a small step in the loss-reducing direction, step size = learning rate
- Repeat: forward pass → compute loss → nudge weights → repeat
- After thousands of iterations, weights converge to values that produce low loss on new data
:::

## Backpropagation: Sharing the Blame {.center}

- After a prediction, the error signal travels **backwards** through the network
- Each weight receives a signal: "you contributed *this much* to the error"
- All weights are updated at once, efficiently

> The network learns by repeatedly asking: "what would I need to change to do better next time?"

::: notes
- Backpropagation sends the error signal backwards through the network after a forward pass
- Uses the chain rule to calculate how much each weight contributed to the loss
- Gives the gradient for every weight in one efficient backward pass
- In PyTorch, a single `loss.backward()` call does all of this automatically
:::

# Why "Deep" Matters {background-color="#1a252f"}

## Layers Build on Layers {.center}

| Depth | What the network detects |
|-------|--------------------------|
| Layer 1 | Edges, intensity gradients, colour transitions |
| Layer 2 | Corners, curves, simple textures |
| Layer 3 | Shapes, repeating patterns |
| Layer 4+ | Complex structures, object parts |

- This **hierarchy** emerges automatically from training, it is not programmed in
- Each layer combines the features from the layer before into something more complex

::: notes
- Deep networks discover a feature hierarchy automatically, they are not programmed in
- The structure emerges because it is the most efficient way to represent the training data
- The same hierarchy appears across different networks trained on different datasets
- Depth enables this: a shallow network can only represent simple mappings; depth builds abstraction
:::

## From Pixels to Predictions {.center}

```{mermaid}
graph LR
  A["150,528 pixel values"] --> B["Edges and colour gradients"] --> C["Vessel structure and textures"] --> D["Lesion patterns and global features"] --> E["Disease / No disease"]
```

- The network discovers what to look for, features are not hand-engineered
- The relevant features for retinopathy emerge from training on labelled images
- **This is what makes deep learning powerful on complex, high-dimensional data**

::: notes
- Traditional ML: a domain expert decides what features to extract (vessel diameter, lesion count, etc.)
- Deep learning: the network discovers what to look for automatically
- Emergent features often outperform hand-crafted alternatives
- Core promise: automatic, scalable feature learning directly from raw data
:::

# Key Takeaways {background-color="#1a252f"}

## The Intuition Behind the Math {.center}

- **Neurons and Weights** — A neuron computes a weighted sum of its inputs; weights are the network's memory.
- **Layers and Depth** — Neurons form layers; layers form networks; depth enables complex representations.
- **Activation functions** — ReLU introduces non-linearity, each additional layer adds genuine complexity.
- **The Forward Pass** — Data flows from pixels through layers to a prediction, one direction only.
- **Loss Functions** — Measure how wrong the prediction is; cross-entropy penalises confident errors hardest.
- **Gradient Descent and Backpropagation** — The network learns by repeatedly nudging weights in the loss-reducing direction.
- **Why Depth Matters** — Feature hierarchies (edges → shapes → structures) emerge automatically from training.
